items.plain: A test score for an artificial intelligence program means little if it saw the answers or the grading was altered. This component is given three example records of test runs, the locked grading rules, and evidence of which files each run opened and whether test material leaked in. It checks that each record names the locked grader and settings, works out whether the run kept to the rules, and rejects any record whose written verdict disagrees. A reader examining how a test claim was recorded can see each verdict, two passes and one set aside in the example.
items.summary: Checks benchmark replay evidence against locked evaluator configuration and recomputed integrity verdicts.
items.title: Benchmark integrity replay

items.plain: An automated assistant's closing report may say it saved its work and passed a test when it did not. This component is given claims in a fixed format about a saved snapshot, a log entry and a test, plus a small example project. It compares the claimed snapshot and log entry with the project's records, runs the named test, and accepts a pass claim only if the test succeeded and the claim says the result was checked. The output lists which claims held up and whether the test passed, so a reader can compare a closing report with what happened.
items.summary: Checks fixture commit, ledger and test claims using a temporary Git repository and a pytest subprocess.
items.title: Audit claims about a completed task

items.plain: A memory-keeping assistant must decide when to add, change or delete an entry, especially when new facts clash with old. This component is given a recorded sequence of example memory changes, the clashes between entries, and a later replay of the sequence. It checks that each later edit or deletion rests on an earlier entry, cited evidence and correct timing, and it examines source trust and priority rather than accepting each change's label alone. The output lists the checks and findings, so someone can see which recorded memory changes were backed by evidence.
items.summary: Checks temporal ordering and evidence for memory updates, conflicts and replay.
items.title: Replay memory updates and conflicts

items.plain: A monitor program that watches an automated assistant for problems should be tested against deliberate attempts to fool it. This component is given example records of the watched assistant's actions, the test attacks aimed at the monitor, the monitor's observations, and how flagged problems were handled. It works out again which cases the test attacks cover and what the monitor's verdict should be, then compares both with the recorded labels. The output says whether the evidence meets the example's requirements and lists mismatches, such as a coverage claim with no matching test attack.
items.summary: Recomputes fixture monitor verdicts and probe coverage from recorded evidence.
items.title: Check monitor verdicts against adversarial probes

items.plain: A log of what an automated assistant did is only useful if its entries are consistent. This component is given a saved bundle of events recorded along an assistant's route, with copies of source files. It checks that no party in the events claims more authority than it was given, that each copied file is the one recorded, and, in a broader run, that claimed behaviour changes cite evidence that can be found. The output is a pass or a list of findings, so someone can see which checks a bundle of records fails.
items.summary: Checks recorded route events, actor authority and evidence references.
items.title: Validate recorded agent routes

items.plain: A watching program labels each episode of an automated assistant's work as caught or not caught for pursuing a hidden side goal. This component is given recorded example episodes, the watcher's scores, the assistant's actions and the evidence behind each label. It compares each episode with a rerun that has no side goal but the same main job, and checks that the difference points to the step tied to the side goal. It lists findings, such as an outdated caught label or a comparison that misses that step, so a reader can judge each label.
items.summary: Checks monitor verdicts and counterfactual evidence in recorded episodes.
items.title: Replay monitor evidence and counterfactuals

items.plain: A sandbox is a restricted area where an automated assistant's actions are held to rules. This component is given made-up action requests, each with its kind, risk level and source trust, plus the written decision and recorded changes. It looks up the decision in a fixed table, blocks unfamiliar requests, and checks that blocked actions never ran and allowed ones have change and undo records. It lists each decision and any mismatch, such as an allow label on a request the table blocks. The table lookup is checked by a mathematical proof against written rules.
items.summary: Derives policy decisions for synthetic action records and checks their side-effect receipts.
items.title: Replay sandbox policy decisions

items.plain: When an automated assistant claims to have found and fixed a security weakness, its evidence needs checking. This component is given made-up records of tiny programs, a suspected problem and its fix, tests that expose the problem, and checkers' verdicts. It runs the tests on each program before and after the fix, compares the results with the records' expectations, and works out each checker's verdict itself. It rejects a claimed pass with no test run or a recorded result that differs from the computed one, so a reader can judge the fix's evidence.
items.summary: Checks synthetic vulnerability and patch evidence, including executable regression witnesses.
items.title: Replay a synthetic patch evidence chain

items.plain: A catalogue of entries only helps if a person can find the ones that fit their problem. This ranking tool reads a written problem and a small catalogue, where each entry has routing labels, family text, a summary and notes. It counts the words and phrases the problem shares with each entry, weighting routing labels most, then family text, then summary and notes. It returns a ranked list showing what matched in each entry, so a person can pick the best fit, or reports no match when nothing overlaps or a chosen filter excludes every entry.
items.summary: Ranks a supplied catalogue with explainable weighted keyword and phrase matching.
items.title: Rank a small catalogue by keyword overlap

items.plain: People who write guide documents may want to compare two ways of laying them out. This component is given a scoring program, three made-up tasks, and two sets of guide documents, one flat and one led by the main ideas. It scores each set on each task by the expected references it reaches and rough measures such as step count, and rejects any setting that puts the expected answers into the documents. In the example all three tasks favour the second set, though an audit shows the two sets hold different kinds of documents.
items.summary: Runs and audits a fixture route-comparison scorecard.
items.title: Run a small route-comparison simulation

items.plain: Rules for which changes and releases are allowed only help if they really refuse bad requests. Its input is sample plans and requests, some deliberately broken, plus copies of the rule-checking code. It runs each rule on them, refusing for example a malformed plan for observing then changing something and a choice of what to publish that breaks a hard exclusion, and checks each copy against its record. The output lists each check and its outcome so someone can see which rules behave as intended. One check, which sizes interface lanes, stays blocked as the test expects.
items.summary: Exercises fixture governance and compiler checks and records a deferred binding repair.
items.title: Exercise governance and compiler checks

items.plain: A copied program file can quietly change or go out of date. Its input is a sample set of four copied program files, the fingerprint recorded for each (a short code worked out from its exact contents), and text each file must still contain. It recomputes each fingerprint and compares it with the record, checks the required text, confirms old fingerprints no longer match, and checks that each file is valid program text without running it. The result is a pass or blocked verdict with a summary board, showing whether the copies still match the record.
items.summary: Checks copied Python files against recorded digests and anchors, then compiles them.
items.title: Check copied source for drift

items.plain: Small helper routines in a software project, like one that picks which earlier run of a job to trust, can fail on awkward cases. It is given thirteen checks with sample cases, from choosing between runs of a data feed to checking links and market figures. It runs each check, for example picking a working feed run over a failed one marked as preferred, and blocking a file with a token shaped like a secret key. The output records each exercise and its cases that should fail, so someone can see how each routine behaves.
items.summary: Exercises thirteen selected checks across navigation, research and market data.
items.title: Exercise a collection of source-backed checks

items.plain: A market dashboard can mislead if its data has broken links, unsafe references or stale feeds. This component is given a made-up bundle of dashboard data, covering a queue of situations, a diagram of points and links, and feed status. It rejects a link with no destination or a reference that climbs out of its folder, tells a stale feed from a fresh one, and treats two situations as unrelated when they share no subject and differ in type. It writes a result for each of the three checks and notes how each broken example was handled.
items.summary: Checks synthetic dashboard data, feed freshness and related situations.
items.title: Check a market dashboard read model

items.plain: Prediction markets let people trade on whether an event will happen, and a list of them can repeat a market or hide missing data. This component is given made-up market rows and records of which market is which, plus small test cases for data problems. Among duplicate listings it keeps the row with more trading, totals without double counting, and refuses to invent an identity for a market with no matching record. The output is totals plus data warnings, such as a feed with no rows or a change marked unavailable for lack of an earlier successful run.
items.summary: Exercises copied market-board helpers on synthetic rows and identity records.
items.title: Check prediction-market row aggregation

items.plain: Before a project is released, its documents need checking for risky claims about what the project is or can do. It writes two short sample documents, one warning against claiming the project is open source (its code shared openly) and one plainly claiming it is ready for real-world use. It runs a simplified public stand-in for the original gate, which looks for listed risky phrases in both, and records which phrases matched and what the gate decided. The readiness claim is blocked, so someone can check that the gate catches that kind of wording.
items.summary: Tests a claim-language gate on sample documents with contrasting release claims.
items.title: Test a release claim-language gate

items.plain: Having the code for a proof or permission check is not the same as that check making a decision. The component reads a list of copied program files and a few example cases. It searches the files for the code behind decisions such as rejecting a bundle whose fingerprint does not match, and scans a copied proof file for placeholders standing in for missing proofs. It also checks an example where Erdős problem 257 is wrongly claimed solved and, if the tools are installed, reports whether the proof file builds, fails or could not be tried.
items.summary: This fixture checks source manifests and exercises selected proof, permission and runtime cases.
items.title: Inspect proof and authority boundaries

items.plain: Systems that keep saved records and run programs need safeguards that catch mistakes. It is given made-up cases for saved records and background processes, plus a map of what depends on what. It runs each safeguard on its cases and rejects the bad ones, and for the dependency map it lists everything that relies on a chosen item, directly or indirectly. The output is an outcome for each case, so someone can check each safeguard did what it should. One small step, finding what relies on the chosen item, is checked by a mathematical proof against written rules.
items.summary: Exercises receipt, replay, proof-contract and dependency-impact checks.
items.title: Exercise receipt and execution safeguards

items.plain: Small building blocks inside a large project, like one that picks key phrases out of text, can fail on odd inputs. It is given copies of selected blocks and small made-up cases covering text, money units, tasks running at once, recording timing and more. It runs each block on its cases, and a phrase made only of filler words yields no key phrase while amounts whose unit scales do not match are blocked. Each exercise gets its own result, so someone can see how every block handles these cases.
items.summary: Exercises copied primitives for text, memory, policy, markets and recording timing.
items.title: Exercise text, policy and timing primitives

items.plain: A recording app relies on a few small guards in its code, and an edit could remove one unnoticed. Its input is the program code of the Demo Take recording console. It checks the code for guards such as the rule that a recording needs at least one screen, audio or webcam source, confirms that altered copies with a guard removed are rejected, and tries to build the app without launching it. The output is a short summary of each check, which someone can use to see that the guards are still in place.
items.summary: Checks recording-console source contracts and a Swift build witness.
items.title: Check Demo Take capture contracts

items.plain: Tools that run a software project rely on helper routines to order tasks, apply edits and choose which tests to rerun. It is given copies of such routines and small example cases for each. It runs each routine on its cases, rejecting tasks that depend on one another in a circle, refusing an edit whose surrounding lines do not match, and checking that an empty test choice falls back to a default. The result combines checks on the copied source with each routine's outcome, showing whether they handle these cases as intended.
items.summary: Exercises copied engines for traces, scheduling, patch checks and other workflows.
items.title: Run selected macro-engine exercises

items.plain: A system that produces many output files needs a way to list them and fill gaps. It is given copied code from Oracle, a market-evidence system, and the output files of a small sample run. It lists those files, builds a snapshot, compares an economic data series and tests a plan for filling in files missing from a related run. The plan stays blocked because some inputs it needs are missing, and the output is a set of short summaries of how the copied code behaves on the sample.
items.summary: Exercises copied Oracle modules for artifact indexing, snapshots and comparisons.
items.title: Exercise Oracle indexing and repair planning

items.plain: Market programs rely on small calculations that can go wrong on awkward data. It is given copied code for three such calculations and made-up data to run them on. It measures a stock's momentum, scores a market from four angles, and finds the highest buying price and lowest selling price in an order book, which is a list of offers to buy and sell. The output records each result, including a test book in which taking the first row would be wrong and a price drop so extreme that the formula rejects it.
items.summary: Three copied market primitives are exercised on synthetic data.
items.title: Synthetic market primitives: stock momentum and order books

items.plain: A loudness meter must turn many tiny sound measurements into one number, and this component is a rewrite of that calculation in another programming language. It is given lists of sound measurements, stored as decimals or whole numbers, each with the loudness it should give. For each list it squares the measurements, averages them, takes the square root, multiplies by eight and limits the answer to between zero and one, after dividing whole numbers by 32767. An empty list gives zero, an unknown format is rejected, and the output shows whether the rewrite matches the expected levels.
items.summary: A Python port computes a normalized RMS level for audio samples.
items.title: Calculate a normalized audio level

items.plain: Code copied from one project into another can stop following the rules it came with. This check takes six groups of copied compliance and processing-pipeline code, plus a few small example inputs. It reads each copy to check its stated promises still hold and runs selected helpers, such as shortening a long text that hides one instruction among filler lines, then checking the instruction survives. It also removes an instruction marker from a copy to confirm the check fails, then writes a status with findings showing whether the copies hold up.
items.summary: A fixture checks copied compliance contracts and pipeline helpers.
items.title: Check copied compliance and pipeline helpers

items.plain: Programs that allow or refuse an action need their rules tested on known cases. This check loads three copied decision rules and feeds them made-up cases, including lab result files, an unregistered market situation and campaign status changes. The lab audit flags a summary containing a question mark, the market gate refuses the unregistered situation, and the campaign check allows a move from candidate to blocked but refuses completed back to running. The refusals come from running the copied code, and a saved status reports the outcome.
items.summary: Three copied policy engines decide synthetic cases.
items.title: Exercise three policy decisions

items.plain: A report on investment ideas can look better than it is when it shows only the ideas that worked. This check uses copied finance code to build made-up market claims, including winners, losers and a comparison case that should not count as a success. A validator rejects a set with only winners, and it flags a failed pattern promoted into the ideas to pursue and a comparison case relabeled as a confirmed claim. The output is a status with named findings, which shows whether the rules catch one-sided evidence.
items.summary: A synthetic thesis family tests losses, controls and forward gates.
items.title: Test a structural-thesis family with losses and controls

items.plain: Small helper tools can fail on odd input, so they need trying on known cases. This check loads four copied helpers and gives them small example inputs. It divides the labels from two evidence lists into shared, missed and extra ones, edits a temporary document, tidies names, and notes a badly formed entry as a gap when reading sample files. The result is a status with findings, and the step that divides the labels is checked by a mathematical proof against written rules.
items.summary: Four copied tools run small diff, patch, identity and parsing examples.
items.title: Exercise four copied tooling primitives

items.plain: A pass from a project's checking program means little until someone knows what it was able to check where it ran. This component is given a copy of that checking program's written code. It reports on six groups of checks, such as required markers in the code, and runs the checkers themselves only when the larger system the code was copied from is present. In a public copy it confirms only the required markers and labels the other groups as source-only, so a reader can tell which results come from running checkers.
items.summary: Checker evidence depends on whether parent runtime state is available.
items.title: Inspect validator source and available checker exercises

items.plain: A workflow system has many small mechanisms, and any of them can break when code is copied. This check is given ten public examples, one per mechanism, such as approval claims, fixed software versions and limits on what workers may touch. It runs each mechanism on its example, including bad cases like a plan with a missing target, and checks that the expected source files and key markers are present. It records each exercise so a reader can check the mechanisms still work, and its tests alter the code and inputs to show several verdicts come from running the code.
items.summary: Ten workflow mechanisms are checked on bounded public examples.
items.title: Exercise ten workflow checks

items.plain: When a program is trained with scores for each step and for its final result, careless scoring can reward the wrong things. This component is given made-up records of task attempts, covering the program's beliefs, the feedback it received, the scores awarded and a stored re-run. It follows each link between these records and checks them against a written rule, under which every step score must rest on an automatic checker or observed feedback. It reports a pass or a block with findings, for example rejecting a bypassed checker or a score for neat formatting.
items.summary: Replay checks links and policy constraints in synthetic process-reward records.
items.title: Replay a process-reward record with verifier feedback

items.plain: A program that proposes its own work needs firm limits, so a person can review each proposal first. This component is given a made-up list of gaps in what a project checks, a policy of limits and a ledger of failed plans. It drafts candidate work items for people to review, each naming one gap and none allowed to change code, using the project's plan-building tool in read-only mode, which the public copy inspects rather than runs. It blocks a policy that would allow code changes, an empty draft, or a ledger listing the same failed plan more than once.
items.summary: A synthetic campaign fixture drafts review-only candidates.
items.title: Draft a bounded campaign packet

items.plain: A job split into dependent tasks can be planned badly, for example with tasks waiting on each other in a circle. This component is given a plan listing evidence-gathering steps, optional steps that combine results, and one final step that pulls everything together. It checks that labels are unique, every dependency exists, no chain of dependencies leads back to itself, and a single final step traces back to an evidence-gathering step. It accepts or rejects the plan before any work starts, recalculating from the plan itself rather than trusting a declared status.
items.summary: A campaign graph validator rejects malformed dependency plans.
items.title: Validate a campaign dependency graph

items.plain: Resuming a paused job goes wrong if its resume note is missing or already used. This component reads made-up records of a paused job, its resume note, alive signals, computer-load decisions and skipped workers. It checks that the job paused with its place saved, its note is unused, and a recent alive signal matches the job's stage. It writes five saved records for testing handoff rules, and other cases catch a missing note, a second resume attempt and a stale alive signal that claims too much.
items.summary: Checks synthetic continuation, heartbeat and resume records.
items.title: Check a synthetic bridge continuation

items.plain: Small mathematical claims should be settled by a strict checker, not by taking someone's word. The lab is given small claims about whole numbers, such as 2 + 3 = 5, with some of them deliberately wrong. It builds a small project for Lean, a program that checks mathematical proofs, and has Lean accept or reject each claim, so 2 + 3 = 6 must be refused. The output is a saved record of the build and each result that keeps what Lean accepted apart from other suggestions and leaves out proof text.
items.summary: Checks finite certificate examples with a Lean fixture.
items.title: Run a small Lean certificate lab

items.plain: A list of reusable reasoning procedures can mark an entry as active without any record that it ever changed a decision. This check reads descriptions of each procedure, with a status, and the use records cited for the active ones. It checks each entry has the required fields and a recognised status, and that every active entry's use record cites evidence that can be found. It writes a result and a summary sheet, so a maintainer can find unsupported entries before presenting them as tested.
items.summary: Checks a registry of procedures and cited use records.
items.title: Validate a registry of reusable reasoning procedures

items.plain: The getting-started commands in a project's documentation can go stale as the project changes, and maintainers need to spot which ones have. This check reads a list of those commands, each with links to documentation sections and to saved results of earlier runs. It searches the project's public text for each command, follows each link to its heading, and checks from each saved result that the earlier run passed. For every command it reports whether the text supports it and whether its links and results hold up, so maintainers can fix stale entries.
items.summary: Checks introductory command entries and local references.
items.title: Check quickstart commands and their references

items.plain: People and programs sharing one project can claim the same files, and someone must decide who owns each. This component is given made-up cases of who claimed which files, each claim marked live, stale or unknown. For each automatically generated file it ranks a live claim above an unknown or stale one, even when the stale one came first. It writes advice for each case, such as handing the file to its live owner, releasing stale claims or looking closer. That ranking step is checked by a mathematical proof against written rules.
items.summary: Classifies concurrent-work ownership and closure fixture cases.
items.title: Replay concurrent-work ownership cases

items.plain: A written claim that Mathlib, a large shared library of mathematics, is ready to use can be wrong. The checker is given a saved record of which libraries were available and what each example user needs. It compares those claims with saved evidence and runs a small test in which Lean, a proof-checking program, must load its basic library but fail to load Mathlib with a 'module missing' message. It marks each example user as allowed or blocked and rejects any record that says Mathlib is available without evidence.
items.summary: Checks corpus readiness with source artifacts and a Lean import probe.
items.title: Check corpus readiness and a Mathlib absence case

items.plain: Answering questions about files, such as how many there are, takes a repeatable recipe, and one missing file should not stop the other answers. This component is given a short list of fact recipes and a temporary example folder of files. Each recipe reads one value from a data file, counts files whose names match a pattern, or counts the files a version-tracking tool follows. The output lists each value found, shows a missing file as an error entry instead of stopping, and rejects an unknown kind of recipe.
items.summary: Resolves registry facts by JSON pointer, glob and named callable.
items.title: Resolve facts from a fixture registry

items.plain: A project's written guidance states facts, and the references showing where each comes from can break or fall out of step. This check reads a table of stated facts with their code locations, a map of links between facts, and sample text containing numbers. It compares the declared fact count with the actual rows, checks each fact has a code location and each link ends at a real fact, and flags current-state figures with no matching fact section. It reports broken references and mismatched declarations so maintainers can fix them.
items.summary: Checks fact counts, code locations, graph references and numeric bindings.
items.title: Audit fact references and numeric claims

items.plain: When an automated assistant says its work was saved to a project's history, its records should back that up. This component is given made-up records of the files claimed, the checks and save attempt, and the project's latest version before and after. It compares each record with a written policy, for example requiring that a claimed save moved the latest version and that the checks ran first. The result passes only if two faulty example records, a claimed save with no change and a save attempted before the checks, are both caught.
items.summary: Checks recorded landing evidence and negative fixtures without executing Git.
items.title: Recorded work landing: check the evidence

items.plain: Automated assistants can leave out things a careful reply needs, such as the reason they stop to ask permission. This component is given example assistant replies, each marked with its expected verdict. It scans each reply for set trigger phrases and marks it red, meaning a violation, when one appears without the phrase that would justify it. It writes a summary, without copying the replies, showing whether good examples pass and bad ones are caught. One small decision step, spotting the phrases and making the red or green call, is checked by a mathematical proof against written rules.
items.summary: Runs phrase-based checks against response fixtures and records expected positives and negatives.
items.title: Audit example agent responses

items.plain: A toolkit built from small modules needs a way to see whether they still cover everything it should. This check is given a list of modules, an example exercise for each, the capabilities the set should cover, and a bad case naming a capability that does not exist. An audit goes through the modules, their exercises and the capabilities they cover, and the outcome is compared with what was expected, including catching the missing capability. It writes a result and validation record, and its tests show that changing one module's example changes the combined result.
items.summary: Runs a controller audit and fixture composition over Engine Room modules.
items.title: Run the Engine Room fixture composition

items.plain: A project's written rules and explanatory pages should follow a fixed format. This check reads a list of the written rules, a set of short pages and some deliberately flawed example inputs. It checks that every rule and page has the required fields and that its references lead somewhere real, and it expects to catch the flawed examples, such as a rule name used twice with conflicting definitions. It writes a list of findings and a summary of what it covered, so problems can be found and fixed.
items.summary: Validate fixture standards and paper-module grammar, including negative cases.
items.title: Validate standards and paper-module grammar

items.plain: When forecasting methods are compared on a short record, the best one may have been lucky. This component reads made-up error scores for a baseline method and several candidate methods over 40 occasions, plus a policy on what results may claim. It runs standard statistical tests, several by re-drawing the scores at random 40 times, to judge whether differences between the methods are bigger than luck would explain. The output is each test's result, or a clear refusal when a setup lets a forecast see later data.
items.summary: Evaluate synthetic forecast-loss fixtures and boundary checks.
items.title: Evaluate synthetic forecast losses

items.plain: A claimed answer to one finite case of the fraction sum in Erdős problem 257 can be checked by redoing it exactly. The input is a short list of positive whole numbers, a base of at least 2, and the claimed values. For each number n it adds 1 divided by (base to the power n, minus 1), finds the smallest power of the base leaving a remainder of 1 when divided by the sum's bottom number, and compares that power with the list's least common multiple. It recomputes the claimed values and rejects a forged bottom number or power.
items.summary: Compute and check a finite rational denominator and multiplicative-order certificate.
items.title: Check a finite denominator and multiplicative order

items.plain: Each claim in a research paper should point to real evidence and to a findable place in public files. The resolver reads the paper's claims, evidence records and a list of named places in public source files. It checks that every claim names an evidence record that exists, that each file and marked spot it cites can be found, and that imported copies match their stored fingerprints. It saves a record of what resolved and rejects deliberately bad example claims, such as a missing cited place, a reference to private material and human approval treated as proof.
items.summary: Resolve claims to public evidence cells and source markers.
items.title: Resolve evidence cells to public source anchors

items.plain: Saying a proof was checked is different from showing that a checking program really ran on it. The component takes a small public project of very simple example theorems and needs Lean, a program that checks proofs, and its build tool, Lake. It runs both on the project and records each outcome, then checks that a wrong proof is rejected and that a file importing a forbidden library, Mathlib, is turned away. The result is a short saved record of those outcomes, usable as evidence that the checker really ran.
items.summary: Record Lean and Lake results for a small public proof fixture.
items.title: Run a Lean and Lake proof witness

items.plain: Proving a statement relies on earlier results, which must be found among many. It is given short public descriptions of known results, without proofs, and a query of keywords for what is to be proved. It scores each description by how many keywords it shares with the query, adds a bonus for a matching strategy tag, drops disallowed ones, and sorts from highest score to lowest. The result is a ranked shortlist, checked against the list the example expects, and inputs carrying a full proof are rejected. One small step, the scoring and sorting, is checked by a mathematical proof against written rules.
items.summary: Rank public premise metadata by query terms and strategy tags.
items.title: Rank public premise metadata for a query

items.plain: Declared facts about a proof setup, such as which tools work, need checking before anything relies on them. The gate reads declarations of available libraries and proof techniques, a list of known results, routes from kinds of goals to techniques, and size-limited plans for background material. It rejects availability claims with no passing test, routes using unavailable techniques, and entries or plans that hold finished proofs or exceed their size limit. It writes a readiness summary and a saved validation record; in the example, Mathlib, a large shared library of mathematics, is reported unavailable.
items.summary: The readiness gate checks declared formal-math inputs before a proof workflow consumes them.
items.title: Formal Math Readiness Gate

items.plain: A failed proof attempt can be patched and declared fixed without anyone checking it again. The validator reads saved records of proof attempts, the proof checker's logs, the repairs and any success claim. It ties each failure to a repair and requires every success claim to point to a separate re-check of the repaired attempt in the saved records. It also tests a toy repair on 0, 1, 2 and 7, correcting the wrong claim that adding zero to a number gives zero, and writes a validation record.
items.summary: This validator examines recorded attempt, verifier trace, repair, and promotion metadata.
items.title: Formal Math Verifier Trace Repair Loop

items.plain: Files made automatically from other files can fall out of step with their sources. This check is given example setups, each naming source files, the files generated from them, and a check that changes nothing. It fingerprints the sources and generated files, reuses an earlier clean result if the fingerprint matches, and otherwise checks that each generated file exists and runs the setup's own check. It reports the outcome, leaving every file as it found it, and treats a missing file as out of step even when the setup's own check passes.
items.summary: This runtime exercises a generated-file drift gate using fixture owners.
items.title: Generated Projection Drift Runtime

items.plain: Instructions hidden in a document or tool result can trick an automated assistant into obeying them. This component is given made-up records of information moving from documents and tool outputs to actions or answers, with trust labels and verdicts noted. It follows each chain, works out the trust labels carried along it (called taint) and compares them with the recorded labels and verdicts. It rejects untrusted output promoted to an instruction, or flowing unchecked into an action needing special permission. One small decision step, tracing untrusted material and deciding whether to block, is checked by a mathematical proof against written rules.
items.summary: This replay checks synthetic records of information moving from documents and tool output to actions or answers.
items.title: Indirect Prompt-Injection Information-Flow Replay

items.plain: A proof-finding program can look good by cheating, so its proofs need checking. The lab is given two tiny logic statements, such as that two true statements are true together, and needs Lean, a program that checks proofs. It searches step by step, within limits, for a proof of each statement, has Lean check every candidate, and compares the result with a simpler method. The result is pass or fail, or 'locked' if Lean is missing, meaning nothing was checked, and cheats such as answer-key fields, proofs resting on placeholders or extra assumptions, and searches that memorize problem names are rejected. The packaged version instead checks that its three required files are present.
items.summary: This lab runs bounded symbolic search on small Lean propositions and checks candidate proofs with Lean.
items.title: Lean Proof Search Lab

items.plain: A program that helps write proofs needs an index of known facts that matches its source and gives away no answers. This component is given such an index for the standard library of the proof-checking program Lean, listing each fact's name, source and allowed uses, plus copied source details. It matches entries to those details, checks that source files still match their stored fingerprints, and rejects entries from the Mathlib library, leaked proofs or answer keys, and tuning on the test portion. It reports a pass when the checks are met, and a mismatch flags a change to the copied index.
items.summary: Validates public Lean and Std premise descriptors against source metadata.
items.title: Lean/Std Premise Index

items.plain: A reviewer needs to know what was copied into a public project, from where, and how it was checked. This check reads a record for each import, naming its source and target, the checks done and a digest, meaning a fingerprint of the exact content. It rejects a claimed exact copy that lacks a target and a real digest, rejects an import lacking required checking, and can flag a source that changed since the recorded copy. It produces a plan or validation record for a reviewer, and the plan can be previewed without writing any files.
items.summary: This protocol checks records for copying or refactoring selected source material into the public repository.
items.title: Projection Import Protocol

items.plain: When software picks which material a lab should test next, someone should check that the pick follows from the scores. This component reads made-up records of candidate materials, simulated lab tests, safety screening and the candidate declared as chosen. It works out the pick again from a stand-in test score, a score for what to test next and a safety score, then compares it with the declared pick. It writes a result with findings and rejects a pick that no longer matches the scores or a claimed hands-on lab procedure.
items.summary: This validator reads synthetic candidate, simulator assay, safety-screen, and selection records.
items.title: Materials Chemistry Simulator Safety Replay

items.plain: Before proving a statement, someone must pick a first approach, and a program can suggest one by scoring each option. This component is given problem descriptions, such as a statement worded 'if and only if', and strategy cards listing clues for and against each approach. It recalculates each score, adding points for matching clues, subtracting points for opposing clues and adding a small capped bonus for matching search words. It outputs the highest-scoring approach as a hypothesis to try before any proof attempt, or a recorded no-match, and rejects a declared choice that disagrees with it.
items.summary: Scores public problem features against strategy cards to select a first strategy.
items.title: Mathematical Strategy Atlas

items.plain: Changes an automated assistant makes with outside tools should be approved and reversible. This component is given made-up records of tool use, a read-only lookup, a ticket update that changes data and an untrusted source of results. It checks each call for a declared tool, stated permissions and, for any change, that an approval and a way to undo it are recorded. It accepts or rejects each call, for example rejecting an approved change with no way to undo it. One small decision step, the accept or reject call, is checked by a mathematical proof against written rules.
items.summary: This replay validates synthetic MCP-like tool records.
items.title: MCP Tool Authority Replay

items.plain: A claim about which input feature mattered most to a computer model's answer can go stale when the model's numbers change. This component is given a tiny made-up model written as plain numbers, plus a claim naming the top feature and a diagram of connections. It runs the model and measures how much the output changes when each feature is nudged and when it is removed. The result records whether the claimed top feature agrees with those measurements, and it rejects a stale claim or a disconnected diagram.
items.summary: Checks feature attribution in a public fixture and small numerical model.
items.title: Circuit attribution replay

items.plain: A queue of jobs for programs to work on can contradict itself, for example a job marked as running that has no run on record. This component is given made-up queue scenarios, each run in a temporary database, such as lending a job out and recovering it when the loan expires. A checker then compares the job, run and log records against its consistency rules and reports whether the outcome matches what each scenario expects. Where a contradiction is planted on purpose, success means the expected rule fires.
items.summary: Runs temporary SQLite queue cases and checks their reconciliation outcomes.
items.title: Queue reconciliation in a temporary SQLite store

items.plain: Workers saving changes to one project can claim the same files or build on an outdated version. This component reads a made-up example of workers' claims on files, the project version each expected, which tasks wait on which, and rules for a limited save. It lists the active claims, compares each with its files and expected version, and tests whether finished tasks unlock waiting ones and the save rules are met. The output is a verdict with findings, and it rejects a claim built on an outdated version or two claims on one file.
items.summary: Checks work-transaction claims, dependencies and checkpoint policy in a public fixture.
items.title: Work-landing transaction replay

items.plain: A guide that suggests where to start a task can pick a wrong first step or wrong items. This benchmark reads sample routes, each with a first command, chosen items, a summary and the time taken, plus what the task expected. It counts how many expected items were chosen and how many chosen items were relevant, flags forbidden first steps, and compares the time taken with a budget. Each route gets a verdict, checked against the expected one, with delay recorded apart from whether its items were enough. One small counting and decision step is checked by a mathematical proof against written rules.
items.summary: Scores route packets against task-specific artifacts, rules and time budgets.
items.title: Route-packet fitness benchmark

items.plain: A list of suggested ways to dig deeper into a project can go stale or include an option with no command. This check reads the options, each meant to name a command, plus a note recording a fingerprint (a short code that changes if the list changes) and a row count. It rejects an option without a command, compares the fingerprint and count with the list, and refuses a derived summary that claims to be current when they differ. It writes a status and a list of problems, so a maintainer can see what needs fixing.
items.summary: Checks public route rows and records that bind them to an entry route, then writes a validation receipt.
items.title: Navigation route-plane validation

items.plain: Work that has been finished and added to a project should end with a recorded decision about what to improve, if anything. This check reads a list of finished components, each with a closing decision pointing to a saved record of an improvement or of why none was needed. It follows each pointer and rejects a finished component with no closing decision, a dead pointer, or a local improvement claiming to change the project's overall guidance. It writes a validation record, so maintainers can see which finished work lacks a proper closing decision.
items.summary: Checks landed components for linked, same-lane closeout decisions.
items.title: Pattern assimilation closeout check

items.plain: A reusable pattern should be tied to the written rule that governs it, to its sources and to its limits. This check reads pattern entries that each name the governing rule, source references and limits, plus records of where its authority comes from. It rejects entries with missing fields or references, conflicting duplicates, private source text, or public claims that go beyond their evidence. It writes a validation result and related saved records, so a maintainer can see which pattern entries are consistent.
items.summary: Validates pattern bindings, source references and authority records.
items.title: Pattern binding validation

items.plain: A price prediction is graded unfairly if the grading uses evidence from after the prediction was made. This component is given a made-up packet of predictions, the evidence cited for each, and rows recording the realised outcomes. It checks each prediction's target and evidence dates, works out the numeric rankings again and grades the realised direction of each outcome. It writes a result and rejects an outcome with no matching prediction, a grade that disagrees with the one it works out, and later evidence used as if it came earlier.
items.summary: Compares synthetic predictions with supplied evidence and outcomes.
items.title: Prediction and oracle reconciliation

items.plain: A system that changes things automatically needs evidence that each change was checked, allowed by policy and can be undone. This component is given made-up change proposals, each linked to proof records, policy rulings, an undo record and a version-control record. It looks up each record, recalculates a fingerprint summarizing the evidence, checks the version-control record, and rejects a proposal with only one visible policy ruling, a stale fingerprint or no undo record for a reversible write. It writes a saved record of whether each proposal's evidence holds together, showing which are properly backed.
items.summary: Checks synthetic mutation proposals against proof, policy, rollback and replay records.
items.title: Governed mutation evidence replay

items.plain: Diagnostic reports about proofs are only useful if their claims point to real files that have not changed. This component is given a bundle of diagnostic entries, each linking a failure report to a spot in a saved record, plus the source files and their fingerprints. It follows each link to the file and spot it names, compares fingerprints, and rejects any row from an outside provider that contains a full proof. It writes a result without proof text, listing which evidence is supported and flagging any changed source file as out of date.
items.summary: Checks in a public evidence bundle point to source files and receipt anchors.
items.title: Check proof diagnostic evidence

items.plain: An assistant program can take in only so much text at once, so what it is given must be chosen to fit. This component is given ordered recipes listing sections of material, each with its text or a stated size, and a size limit. It goes down each list adding a section only if it fits in the space left, and skips any that do not. The result lists included and left-out sections with sizes but not text, so a reader can see what was dropped. One small decision step, whether a section fits, is checked by a mathematical proof against written rules.
items.summary: Packs ordered context sections within a byte budget and reports omissions.
items.title: Pack context sections within a byte budget

items.plain: A public walkthrough can make claims that nothing in it backs up. This check reads a walkthrough's steps, each naming a command, something to inspect and a reference to evidence, plus a declared time budget. It rejects a walkthrough with a budget over ten minutes, fewer than five steps, too few different commands or evidence references, or a step missing a part. It writes a summary sheet and a list of problems, helping a reader follow each claim to its evidence. One small decision step is checked by a mathematical proof against written rules.
items.summary: Checks walkthrough claims and their links to public evidence.
items.title: Check a public walkthrough against its evidence

items.plain: When a team says it repeated a study's results, a reader needs evidence that the repeat was run and not described. This component reads made-up replay records listing a study's contributions, scoring checklist, output files, scoring script and rerun evidence. It compares the declared fingerprints of the output files, short codes that change when a file changes, with those of the rerun, and adds up the input rows itself to check the one supported score. The output lists findings and rejects a record that cites a file nobody declared or leans on a report with no rerun.
items.summary: Checks research replay records and recomputes the supported sum-field metric against declared artifacts.
items.title: Check a research replication record

items.plain: A tool that suggests facts for a proof can be scored on how well its suggestions match what the proof needed. This component is given, for each problem, the tool's ranked suggestions, with a fixed number of places, and a separate list of the facts needed. It counts the needed facts found, then computes precision, the share of places holding a needed fact, and recall, the share of needed facts found. It reports both for each problem and overall, so the tool can be judged, and rejects any row that admits using the answer key.
items.summary: This harness compares retrieved premise rankings with separately supplied needed-premise labels.
items.title: Measure premise retrieval against labelled examples

items.plain: A list of common mistakes in choosing where to go next for a task should name each expected mistake once and explain it. This check reads that list, saved as a data file, with a name and a written explanation for each mistake. It checks that the list declares its type and version, includes every required mistake, repeats no identifier and has no empty explanation. It writes findings and a summary sheet for a maintainer to act on, and the example set includes broken lists it must catch.
items.summary: The input is a JSON registry of named routing mistakes and explanatory text.
items.title: Validate a routing anti-pattern registry

items.plain: A project keeps a map of its own parts, and some parts it knows exist may be missing from the map. This comparison reads counts and identifiers for categories such as concepts and standards, plus a saved map that represents some of them. For each category it works out the shortfall between the listed count and the number shown on the map, and checks that required identifiers are present. The shortfall, called coverage debt, points to known gaps, and a claim that a missing entry shows something does not exist is rejected.
items.summary: The exported bundle contains kind-atlas rows and a materialized system graph.
items.title: Compare known atlas coverage

items.plain: Running the same command again and again wastes time when nothing it depends on has changed. This component is given a command runner and temporary example commands to run through it as local processes. For each request it builds a label from the command, its folder, the project's state, the contents of the files that matter and a few settings, so requests with the same label can share one run. The output is a saved result showing which requester ran the command and which reused its answer, and a change to one of those files gives a new label.
items.summary: Exercises command-run deduplication using keys derived from inputs and environment.
items.title: Deduplicate matching local command runs

items.plain: An assistant with long-term memory can save a poisoned note that does harm when retrieved later. This component is given made-up records, holding references rather than the notes themselves, of a poisoned write, its quarantine, a later retrieval and a rollback, meaning removal. It checks where the memory came from and the links between the quarantined note, the retrieval check, the quarantine decision record and the re-run record. The output lists findings, and a retrieval that admits a quarantined note or fails to cite that decision record is rejected.
items.summary: This replay examines public metadata for a poisoned memory write, quarantine, later retrieval and rollback.
items.title: Check a memory quarantine and rollback record

items.plain: A prediction of how a scene will change after a 'what if' event goes out of date when the scene or event changes. This component is given made-up scenes on a small grid, each with a 'what if' event and a predicted scene afterwards. For each one it works out the grid's next step under fixed rules, then compares the number of actors and the other changes with the prediction. The output is a list of findings showing each mismatch, and a prediction that no longer matches the computed step is rejected.
items.summary: Compares predicted counterfactual transitions with a deterministic toy gridworld.
items.title: Compare a predicted transition with a toy gridworld

items.plain: Each accepted component of a project should have a written standard, a command that runs it and saved records backing what is said about it. This check reads the project's public list of accepted components, along with inventory and command entries, and some deliberately flawed example inputs. It compares accepted components with those entries, checks that each cited standard and saved record exists, and rejects a claim of permission to release. It writes a result listing what it found, so maintainers can see which components lack standards or references.
items.summary: Checks accepted components for declared standards, commands and receipt references.
items.title: Standards coverage diagnostics

items.plain: Lean, a program that checks proofs, has automatic methods called tactics, and which of them work depends on the setup. This component is given a table of tactics with their recorded outcomes, timings and environment details, such as whether the Mathlib library was present, plus the original test files behind them. It checks the table against those files, rejecting a tactic called available with no recorded outcome and a Mathlib claim with no evidence. The output is an availability report that a later step can use when choosing which tactic to try.
items.summary: Summarizes recorded tactic availability, timing and environment.
items.title: Tactic availability from recorded probes

items.plain: Different kinds of statement call for different automatic proof methods, called tactics, so a program must choose among them. This component is given notes on which tactics are available and example cases giving a statement's shape, the candidates and the tactic chosen. It checks each choice against availability and the preferences for that shape, and requires a fallback when the shape is unknown or the preferred tactic is unavailable. It writes a routing report for use before a proof attempt. The small step that picks the first usable preferred tactic is checked by a mathematical proof against written rules.
items.summary: Checks tactic choices against recorded availability and target-shape preferences.
items.title: Choose tactics for a target shape

items.plain: When too many programs are running on a computer, someone has to work out which ones belong to whom. This check is given a saved snapshot of the running programs, a list classifying their owners and a policy on how much pressure is too much. It follows ownership links, sorts owners into active, unknown and detached, applies the policy, and rejects any claim that a program with an unknown owner is safe to close. The output is an inventory and a recommendation for easing the pressure, to help decide what needs an owner's attention.
items.summary: Classifies supplied tool-server processes and recommends pressure relief.
items.title: Classify tool-server process pressure

items.plain: A proof attempt may lean on a library fact that was never declared as allowed. This component is given records of proof attempts, each listing the library names used, the facts allowed and the facts cited, plus an index of known facts. Citing a fact outside the allowed list counts as a budget violation and takes priority; otherwise a known full library name on neither list counts as undeclared. Each record gets an advisory label and a review outcome, showing someone which attempts leaned on facts nobody had listed.
items.summary: Classifies observed library symbols against allowed and cited premise IDs.
items.title: Classify undeclared library symbols

items.plain: A fair test of an automatic prover must run its steps for real, with no answers leaking in. This component is given a small public project for Lean, a proof-checking program, with recorded proof steps, a retry that supplies a missing fact, and a proposed change to failure handling. It runs Lean on the project, rejecting steps that expose a full proof or let comparison notes or provider suggestions in, and any change that claims unlimited power over source files. It writes saved records of the run and the checks, without candidate proofs, showing whether the inputs pass or are blocked.
items.summary: Checks verifier transitions and policy candidates; the direct fixture runs Lean.
items.title: Run the bounded verifier-lab execution spine

items.plain: Testing an automatic prover goes wrong if a comparison note is counted as the prover's success or an outside suggestion is counted as a proof. This component is given results from smaller checks and a packet of public problems, comparison notes, provider hypotheses and proposed actions. It checks these against the packet's rules and rejects a comparison result counted as a success, a provider hypothesis claiming to be a proof, and full proofs where none belong. The output is a pass or blocked status with findings, showing whether the parts of this test keep their roles apart.
items.summary: Checks verifier-lab fixtures, keeping oracle and provider data separate from forward results.
items.title: Inspect the verifier-lab kernel

items.plain: A lesson learned on a project should reach whoever owns the relevant guidance, be checked and be closed out. This check reads a policy for how lessons may spread, plus records naming each lesson's trigger, owner, action, check and closing step. It follows each reference, compares each lesson with the allowed sequence, and rejects a lesson promoted project-wide without its owner's check. It writes a report with no private text so the records can be inspected, and it rejects raw spoken remarks or private discussions in the input.
items.summary: This validator checks public records that connect a local lesson to an owner surface, validation and closeout.
items.title: Validate a lesson-to-owner record

items.plain: A public view built from source material can stop agreeing with the source. This check takes the rules for building the view, the declared public source evidence and a saved list of mismatches, each tying a source signal to a target, a proposed repair and a check. It recomputes the mismatches from the rules and evidence, compares them with the saved list, checks saved records of the source and of a running program, and rejects entries missing a source or check reference. The output is a report of these checks, showing whether the view still agrees with the evidence.
items.summary: Recomputes public projection-drift rows and compares them with a supplied snapshot and supporting evidence.
items.title: Check projection-drift records
